helper.py:

    def caller():

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

## Revised Implementation Approach

### 1. Extend `_parse_imports` — return two maps instead of one

```python
def _parse_imports(tree):
    from_import_map = {}   # existing: name → module  (from X import Y)
    module_import_map = {} # new:      alias → module (import X / import X as Y)
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom) and node.module:
            for alias in node.names:
                from_import_map[alias.asname or alias.name] = node.module
        elif isinstance(node, ast.Import):
            for alias in node.names:
                local_name = alias.asname if alias.asname else alias.name

```

The existing function already appends `n.func.attr` for every non-`self` attribute call. For `helper.helper()` that means `"helper"` lands in `func.calls`. **We do not change this function at all.**

---

### 3. `build_repo_graph` — add one new resolution branch

Today the resolution loop is:

```python

    if call_name in standalone_names:
        graph.add_edge(...)
    elif call_name in import_map and import_map[call_name] in known_modules:
        graph.add_edge(...)
```

# Create Plan

Follow this structured workflow to produce a high-quality, actionable plan.

## Step 1 — Gather Requirements

Ask the user clarifying questions to fully understand the task:
- What is the goal and expected outcome?
- Are there constraints, preferences, or non-goals?
- Which parts of the codebase are likely involved?
- Any related issues or requirement documents?

Do not proceed until you have enough context to scope the work, be critical of vague intent or requirements.

## Step 2 — Code Search via Sub-Agent

Spawn a `spawn_subagent` of type `"explore"` to research the codebase. The sub-agent should:
- Locate relevant files, symbols, and patterns related to the task
- Identify existing utilities or abstractions that should be reused
- Identify existing design patterns
- Surface any constraints or conventions (e.g. patterns in similar files)

Use the sub-agent's findings to ground your plan in the actual code.

## Step 3 — Clarify Design Intention

Based on the requirements and code research:
- Always confirm your understanding of the intended design with the user
- Raise any open questions or trade-offs that need a decision
- Adjust scope if the code research revealed complexity or simplifications

Do not begin writing the plan document until design intent is confirmed.

## Step 4 — Write the Plan File

Write a structured plan to a markdown file (e.g. `{short-plan-name}-plan.md`). The plan must NOT go into low-level code detail — focus on *what* needs to happen and *why*.

The plan file must include:

### Top-Level Overview
A concise summary of the goal, scope, and approach.

### Sub-Tasks
Break the work into sub-tasks. Each sub-task must have:
- **Intent** — what this sub-task achieves and why
- **Expected Outcomes** — observable results when this sub-task is complete
- **Todo List** — ordered, specific steps to achieve the outcome
- **Relevant Context** — pointers to relevant files, symbols, or patterns
- **Status** — `[ ] pending` (updated to `[x] done` after completion)

Design each sub-task to be processed independently, one at a time, so changes stay focused and reviewable.

## Step 5 — Plan Validation

Before moving to implementation, ensure that the user has fully read the plan. Always ask the user targeted questions to verify the plan is correct and complete:
- Does this plan capture the full scope of the task?
- Are the sub-task boundaries and ordering correct?
- Is any context missing that would be needed during implementation?

Use Mermaid diagrams in chat responses where they clarify architecture or workflow, but do not place Mermaid diagrams directly in the plan file. Avoid double quotes and parentheses inside square brackets in Mermaid syntax.

Refine the plan file based on the user's answers.

## Step 6 — Implementation

Only after the user confirms the plan, recommend implementation by calling the `switch_mode` tool to `agent`.

When explaining how to implement the plan in agent mode:
- Using the `start_subtask` tool, create a new task for each subtask in the <plan-file>.
- In the prompt for the subtask make sure it reads the plan-file to gain the full context around the task.
- After each sub task is complete update the task status in the <plan-file>
- Add any context needed for the next subtask in the <plan-file>
- Wait for the user to check and ok the changes before moving on to the next subtask.

## Reminders

- Ask questions always using the "ask_followup_question" tool
- Never include information without evidence
- Don't include time estimates

1 | """
2 | Day 13 -- ContextGuard project
3 | --------------------------------
4 | Goal: given one function (e.g. one that was just changed), find every
5 | other function within N hops of it in the dependency graph -- counting
6 | BOTH directions: what it calls, and what calls it.
7 | 
8 | This is a direct application of BFS, exactly as you've used it in DSA --
9 | just applied to a real dependency graph instead of a textbook grid or tree.
10 | """
11 | 
12 | from collections import deque
13 | 
14 | from day8_function_calls import find_functions_with_calls
15 | from day11_adjacency_list import build_adjacency_list
16 | from day12_networkx_graph import build_networkx_graph

19 | def find_within_hops(graph, start_node, max_hops=2):
20 |     """
21 |     Returns a dictionary mapping every function within `max_hops` steps
22 |     of `start_node` to its exact distance (1, 2, ... up to max_hops).
23 |     `start_node` itself is not included in the result.
24 | 
25 |     Counts BOTH successors (what a function calls) and predecessors
26 |     (what calls it) as valid steps -- we care about both directions
27 |     of influence for code review context.
28 |     """
29 | 
30 |     # visited tracks every node we've reached so far, and how many hops
31 |     # it took to get there. Starting node is distance 0 from itself.
32 |     visited = {start_node: 0}
33 | 
34 |     # deque works like a list, but is efficient for adding to one end
35 |     # and removing from the other -- exactly what a BFS queue needs.
36 |     queue = deque([start_node])
37 | 
38 |     while queue:
39 |         current_node = queue.popleft()  # take the next node to expand
40 |         current_distance = visited[current_node]
41 | 
42 |         # Don't expand past our hop limit -- once we're already at
43 |         # max_hops, there's no point looking at this node's neighbors,
44 |         # since they'd be max_hops + 1 away.
45 |         if current_distance >= max_hops:
46 |             continue
47 | 
48 |         # Gather neighbors in BOTH directions: what this function calls,
49 |         # and what calls this function.
50 |         outgoing = list(graph.successors(current_node)) if current_node in graph else []
51 |         incoming = list(graph.predecessors(current_node)) if current_node in graph else []
52 |         neighbors = outgoing + incoming
53 | 
54 |         for neighbor in neighbors:
55 |             if neighbor not in visited:
56 |                 visited[neighbor] = current_distance + 1
57 |                 queue.append(neighbor)
58 | 
59 |     # Remove the starting node itself from the result -- we only want
60 |     # to report OTHER functions near it, not itself.
61 |     del visited[start_node]
62 | 
63 |     return visited

4 | Goal: properly detect class methods (qualified as "ClassName.method"),
5 | and resolve self.method() calls specifically to other methods of the

14 | def get_ordinary_call_names(function_node):
15 |     """
16 |     Returns ordinary (non-self) calls made inside this function/method.
17 | 
18 |     IMPORTANT FIX: earlier this reused day8_function_calls.get_call_names,
19 |     which doesn't know about self.X() calls and includes them here too --
20 |     that caused every self.X() call to be double-counted (once here,
21 |     once in get_self_call_names below). This version explicitly excludes
22 |     self.X() calls, so each call is classified exactly once.
23 |     """
24 |     call_names = []
25 | 
26 |     for node in ast.walk(function_node):
27 |         if isinstance(node, ast.Call):
28 |             func = node.func
29 | 
30 |             if isinstance(func, ast.Name):
31 |                 call_names.append(func.id)
32 | 
33 |             elif isinstance(func, ast.Attribute):
34 |                 is_self_call = (
35 |                     isinstance(func.value, ast.Name) and func.value.id == "self"
36 |                 )
37 |                 if not is_self_call:
38 |                     call_names.append(func.attr)
39 |                 # if it IS a self-call, we deliberately skip it here --
40 |                 # get_self_call_names below is the only place that records it.
41 | 
42 |     return call_names
43 | 
44 | 
45 | def get_self_call_names(function_node):
46 |     """
47 |     Returns a list of method names called specifically as self.X(...)
48 |     inside this function -- a much more specific signal than a generic
49 |     attribute call, since it always means "call another method of this
50 |     same object."
51 |     """
52 |     self_calls = []
53 | 
54 |     for node in ast.walk(function_node):
55 |         if isinstance(node, ast.Call):
56 |             func = node.func
57 |             # We want exactly: an Attribute call (like self.something())
58 |             # where the thing being accessed is a Name node with id "self".
59 |             if (
60 |                 isinstance(func, ast.Attribute)
61 |                 and isinstance(func.value, ast.Name)
62 |                 and func.value.id == "self"
63 |             ):
64 |                 self_calls.append(func.attr)
65 | 
66 |     return self_calls

69 | def find_functions_with_scope(file_path):
70 |     """
71 |     Like Day 8's function finder, but tracks whether each function is a
72 |     standalone function (class_name=None) or a method belonging to a
73 |     specific class (class_name="ClassName") -- and separately records
74 |     self.X() calls.
75 |     """
76 |     with open(file_path, "r") as f:
77 |         source_code = f.read()
78 | 
79 |     tree = ast.parse(source_code, filename=file_path)
80 | 
81 |     functions_found = []
82 | 
83 |     # We deliberately do NOT use ast.walk() at the top level here, because
84 |     # ast.walk() flattens everything and loses the information of WHICH
85 |     # class a method belongs to. Instead we look only at the file's
86 |     # top-level statements (tree.body), and handle classes explicitly.
87 |     for node in tree.body:
88 | 
89 |         if isinstance(node, ast.FunctionDef):
90 |             # A standalone, module-level function.
91 |             functions_found.append(_build_function(node, class_name=None))
92 | 
93 |         elif isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
94 |             # A class -- look at ITS top-level statements for methods.
95 |             class_name = node.name
96 |             for class_child in node.body:
97 |                 if isinstance(class_child, ast.FunctionDef):
98 |                     functions_found.append(_build_function(class_child, class_name))
99 | 
100 |     return functions_found

103 | def _build_function(node, class_name):
104 |     """Small helper: builds one Function object from a FunctionDef node."""
105 |     name = node.name
106 |     params = [arg.arg for arg in node.args.args]
107 |     body_placeholder = f"(defined at line {node.lineno})"
108 |     calls = get_ordinary_call_names(node)
109 |     self_calls = get_self_call_names(node)
110 | 
111 |     return Function(
112 |         name, params, body_placeholder, calls,
113 |         start_line=node.lineno,
114 |         end_line=node.end_lineno,
115 |         class_name=class_name,
116 |         self_calls=self_calls,
117 |     )

120 | def build_class_aware_edges(functions):
121 |     """
122 |     Builds a list of (source_qualified_name, target_qualified_name) edges,
123 |     correctly handling both:
124 |       - ordinary calls to standalone functions (resolved by plain name,
125 |         same as Day 11)
126 |       - self.X() calls, resolved ONLY to another method in the SAME class
127 |     """
128 |     # Standalone (non-method) functions, by plain name -- for ordinary call resolution.
129 |     standalone_names = {f.name for f in functions if f.class_name is None}
130 | 
131 |     # Methods grouped by class, by plain method name -- for self.X() resolution.
132 |     methods_by_class = {}
133 |     for f in functions:
134 |         if f.class_name:
135 |             methods_by_class.setdefault(f.class_name, set()).add(f.name)
136 | 
137 |     edges = []
138 | 
139 |     for func in functions:
140 |         source = func.qualified_name()
141 | 
142 |         # Ordinary calls: only resolve against standalone functions.
143 |         for call_name in func.calls:
144 |             if call_name in standalone_names:
145 |                 edges.append((source, call_name))
146 | 
147 |         # self.X() calls: only resolve against methods of the SAME class.
148 |         if func.class_name:
149 |             sibling_methods = methods_by_class.get(func.class_name, set())
150 |             for self_call_name in func.self_calls:
151 |                 if self_call_name in sibling_methods:
152 |                     target = f"{func.class_name}.{self_call_name}"
153 |                     edges.append((source, target))
154 | 
155 |     return edges

16 |     def __init__(self, name, params, body, calls=None, start_line=None,

47 | def _get_call_names(node):
48 |     calls = []

110 |         print(f"  [warning] skipping {file_path}: {error}")

116 |             functions.append(_build_function(node, None))
117 |         elif isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):

125 | def build_repo_graph(repo_path):
126 |     """
127 |     Returns (graph, function_lookup). Nodes are fully-qualified names:
128 |     "module.function" or "module.ClassName.method".
129 |     function_lookup maps qualified_name -> (Function, file_path).
130 |     """
131 |     file_data = {}
132 |     for file_path in find_python_files(repo_path):
133 |         module_name = _module_name(file_path)
134 |         functions, import_map = parse_file(file_path)
135 |         file_data[module_name] = {"functions": functions, "import_map": import_map, "file_path": file_path}
136 | 
137 |     known_modules = set(file_data.keys())
138 |     graph = nx.DiGraph()
139 |     function_lookup = {}
140 | 
141 |     for module_name, data in file_data.items():
142 |         functions = data["functions"]
143 |         import_map = data["import_map"]
144 |         standalone_names = {f.name for f in functions if f.class_name is None}
145 |         methods_by_class = {}
146 |         for f in functions:
147 |             if f.class_name:
148 |                 methods_by_class.setdefault(f.class_name, set()).add(f.name)
149 | 
150 |         for func in functions:
151 |             qualified = f"{module_name}.{func.qualified_name()}"
152 |             function_lookup[qualified] = (func, data["file_path"])
153 |             graph.add_node(qualified)
154 | 
155 |             for call_name in func.calls:
156 |                 if call_name in standalone_names:
157 |                     graph.add_edge(qualified, f"{module_name}.{call_name}")
158 |                 elif call_name in import_map and import_map[call_name] in known_modules:
159 |                     graph.add_edge(qualified, f"{import_map[call_name]}.{call_name}")
160 | 
161 |             if func.class_name:
162 |                 siblings = methods_by_class.get(func.class_name, set())
163 |                 for self_call in func.self_calls:
164 |                     if self_call in siblings:
165 |                         graph.add_edge(qualified, f"{module_name}.{func.class_name}.{self_call}")
166 | 
167 |     return graph, function_lookup

170 | def find_within_hops(graph, start_node, max_hops=2):
171 |     """BFS in both directions."""
172 |     visited = {start_node: 0}
173 |     queue = deque([start_node])
174 |     while queue:
175 |         current = queue.popleft()
176 |         distance = visited[current]
177 |         if distance >= max_hops:
178 |             continue
179 |         for neighbor in list(graph.successors(current)) + list(graph.predecessors(current)):
180 |             if neighbor not in visited:
181 |                 visited[neighbor] = distance + 1
182 |                 queue.append(neighbor)
183 |     del visited[start_node]
184 |     return visited

80 | def build_faiss_index(chunks):

83 |     L2-normalized vectors -- mathematically equivalent to cosine similarity,
84 |     but FAISS's actual purpose (and why we use it over brute-force) is
85 |     speed: it scales to large codebases without comparing every pair by hand.

87 |     vectors = np.array([c["embedding"] for c in chunks]).astype("float32")

These then **fail to resolve** against the import map and fall through as external/unknown.

#### D. Dependency Graph Construction and Traversal

**Primary (package):** [`contextguard/graph.py:build_repo_graph()`](contextguard/graph.py:125) and [`find_within_hops()`](contextguard/graph.py:170).

`build_repo_graph()` does a two-pass approach:
1. **First pass:** parse all `.py` files into `file_data` keyed by module name (basename without `.py`).
2. **Second pass:** for each function, create a node `"module.func"` or `"module.Class.method"`, then add edges:
   - Ordinary call → same-file standalone function? → `module.call_name` edge
   - Ordinary call → in `import_map` AND target module is a known repo module? → `import_map[call].call_name` edge
   - `self.X()` → sibling method in same class? → `module.Class.X` edge

`find_within_hops()`: bidirectional BFS (both successors and predecessors) up to `max_hops=2`. Returns `{qualified_name: distance}` excluding the start node.

#### E. Cross-File Import Resolution

**Primary (package):** [`contextguard/graph.py:_parse_imports()`](contextguard/graph.py:69).

Only handles **`from <module> import <name>`** (`ast.ImportFrom`). Maps the local name to its source module. **Plain `import module`** (`ast.Import`) is entirely ignored — no `ast.Import` handler exists in any version.

Resolution in `build_repo_graph()` at lines 158–159: `import_map[call_name] in known_modules` check ensures only intra-repo imports create edges. External library calls (`networkx`, `ast`, etc.) are silently dropped.

### 3. How a Changed Function Connects to Callers and Dependencies

The pipeline in [`contextguard/context.py:build_full_context()`](contextguard/context.py:11):

```
build_repo_graph(repo_path)          → (graph, function_lookup)
find_changed_functions(repo_path, function_lookup)  → [qualified_names]
for each changed_name:
    find_within_hops(graph, changed_name, max_hops=2)  → {neighbor: distance}
```

The graph is a **directed** graph (`nx.DiGraph`). BFS traverses **both directions** (successors = callees, predecessors = callers), so a changed function's callers (reverse edges) are included up to `max_hops` away.

### 4. How Cross-File Calls are Currently Resolved

Only through `from X import Y` statements. If a function calls `helper()` and the file has `from utils import helper`, the import map records `{"helper": "utils"}`. During graph construction, if `"utils"` is in `known_modules` (i.e., there's a `utils.py` in the repo), an edge `current_module.caller → utils.helper` is added.

**What fails:**
- `import utils; utils.helper()` — the call AST is `Attribute(value=Name("utils"), attr="helper")`, which `_get_call_names()` extracts only as `"helper"` (the `.attr`). Then `"helper"` is looked up in `import_map`, but `import_map` only has entries for `from X import Y` style — `import utils` is never parsed — so the edge is silently dropped.
- `from utils import *` — wildcard imports are not handled.
- Relative imports like `from .utils import helper` — `node.module` would be `None` or `".utils"`, which won't match a bare module name in `known_modules`.

### 5. How Imports Are Currently Resolved

[`_parse_imports(tree)`](contextguard/graph.py:69): walks the entire AST tree, finds `ast.ImportFrom` nodes where `node.module` is not None. For each aliased name, maps `alias.asname or alias.name` → `node.module`.

What is **not handled**:
- `import os` (bare `ast.Import`) — completely ignored
- `from . import utils` (relative, `node.module` is `None`) — skipped by the `if node.module:` guard
- `from .subpkg import func` (relative with a `.` prefix) — `node.module` would be `"subpkg"` but `node.level > 0`; there's no `node.level` check, so `"subpkg"` is stored but won't match a top-level `"subpkg.py`" unless it's also a top-level file

### 7. Limitations and Gaps

#### a) Module-Qualified Calls (`module.function()`)

**Confirmed gap.** In [`_get_call_names()`](contextguard/graph.py:47), an `ast.Attribute` call extracts only `node.func.attr` — the bare method name. For a call like `utils.helper()`, this records `"helper"`, which is then looked up in `import_map`. But `import_map` is built only from `from X import Y` — never from `import utils`. So `"helper"` will not be found in `import_map`, and the cross-file edge is silently dropped.

This was deliberately noted as out-of-scope in [`src/day16_cross_file_imports.py`](src/day16_cross_file_imports.py:12–15): *"calls written as `module.function()` … will currently fall into 'external'. That's a reasonable simplification for now, not a silent wrong answer."*

There is **no test** for this case.

#### b) Relative/Package Imports

**Confirmed gap.** `_parse_imports()` only handles `ast.ImportFrom` where `node.module` is not None. The guard `if isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom) and node.module:` skips `from . import utils` (where `node.module` is `None`) entirely. For `from .utils import helper`, `node.module = "utils"` and `node.level = 1`, but the level is not checked — this creates a misleading entry `{"helper": "utils"}` that will resolve against a top-level `utils.py` if one happens to exist, which may be wrong.

Plain `import X` / `import X as Y` (`ast.Import` nodes) are **never parsed at all**, in either `contextguard/graph.py` or `src/graph_builder.py`.

There is **no test** for relative imports.

#### c) Additional Gaps Found

- [`src/retrieval.py`](src/retrieval.py) has a **broken key name**: chunks are stored with `"chunk_id"` key (line 59) but then accessed as `chunk["id"]` (lines 129, 143). This is a latent bug in the `src/` prototype (the `contextguard/retrieval.py` version uses `"name"` consistently).
- Functions inside **nested classes** or **nested functions** are not discovered — `parse_file()` only walks one level deep into class bodies.
- `build_repo_graph()` uses the **basename** of the file as the module name ([`_module_name()`](contextguard/graph.py:36)). In a real package with `src/utils.py` and `lib/utils.py`, both would collapse to module `"utils"`, causing node collisions. The current repo avoids this because all `.py` files have unique names.

### 8. Recommended First Improvement

**Handle `import module` / `import module as alias` to resolve module-qualified calls.**

This is the most impactful single improvement because:
- It is the only gap **explicitly called out in the codebase itself** (day16) as a known limitation to be revisited.
- Real-world Python code extensively uses `import os`, `import re`, `import networkx as nx` — the ContextGuard codebase itself does this (e.g. `import networkx as nx; nx.DiGraph()`).
- Without this, `module.function()` call patterns produce zero edges in the graph, silently reducing call coverage with no warning.
- The fix is minimal and self-contained: extend `_parse_imports()` in [`contextguard/graph.py`](contextguard/graph.py) to also handle `ast.Import` nodes, mapping `alias.asname or alias.name` → the real module name; then in `_get_call_names()`, when an `ast.Attribute` call has `node.func.value` as a `Name` node, check whether that name is in the import map (as a module alias) and, if so, record the full `module.attr` form instead of just `attr`.

#### Exact Files That Would Need Modification

1. **[`contextguard/graph.py`](contextguard/graph.py)** — `_parse_imports()` (add `ast.Import` handling) and `_get_call_names()` (use module alias context when extracting attribute call names) — these two functions are the entire scope of the change.
2. **[`src/graph_builder.py`](src/graph_builder.py)** — the same two functions (`_parse_imports`, `_get_call_names`) if the `src/` prototype is also to be kept consistent.
